questions.prompt: You ask a model for "a caption for my cake business" and get something generic. What is the main reason?
options: The model is not good at writing captions for small food businesses
Your prompt was too short, and longer prompts will always give you better answers
You used a free plan, which gives weaker answers than a paid plan does
It had no facts about your business, so it filled the gaps with the average
questions.explanation: The model knows a lot about cakes and nothing about yours. Context is the facts only you have: who it is for, what you sell, what makes you different.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a constraint, rather than context or a role?
options: "Under 50 words, include the price, and no hashtags."
"You write captions for a home bakery in Lekki, Lagos."
"My customers mostly order birthday cakes at short notice."
"Customers keep telling me my red velvet is not too sweet."
questions.explanation: Constraints set the shape of done: length, format, what must be included and what must be avoided. The others are a role and two pieces of context.

questions.prompt: You have asked for the same thing four times with more words each time, and the answer keeps getting worse. What is the best move?
options: Keep on rewording, because the right combination of words exists and you will find it
Tell the model firmly that it is wrong and ask it to try much harder this time
Stop rewording and change the process: add your own material, or split it into steps
Paste the exact same prompt into a different AI tool and compare the two answers
questions.explanation: The quality comes from a better process, not a better prompt. Arguing with a model instead of directing it is the habit to break.

questions.prompt: Why does asking AI to transform something work better than asking it to create from nothing?
options: Transforming text uses fewer tokens, so the model can spend more effort on quality
From a blank page it has only an average; your rough draft gives it something of yours
Models cannot write anything new, so all they are able to do is rearrange what you give
Short tasks run faster, and a faster answer is usually a more accurate answer too
questions.explanation: A blank page is where generic output comes from. Give it something rough and the result carries your fingerprints, because your material was the input.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to get an honest critique of something AI wrote for you?
options: Paste it into a new chat with no history and ask what is weak
Ask the same conversation to go back and check its own work
Ask the model to give its answer a score out of ten, honestly
Ask it how confident it is, and only trust answers above 90%
questions.explanation: The same conversation defends what it already wrote. A fresh chat has no attachment to the draft, so it gives you the useful answer.

questions.prompt: In the six-role chain, which role do people most often skip, and why does it matter?
options: The Editor, so the writing runs long and repeats itself in places
The Researcher, so the draft has opinions but no facts behind them
The Skeptic, so nobody points out the typos before it all gets posted
The Strategist, so the writing feels like it could be about anything
questions.explanation: The Strategist decides the angle, the audience and what not to say. Skip it and the Writer has nothing to aim at.

questions.prompt: What should a voice skill be built from?
options: A list of adjectives you would like people to use to describe you
Your voice described from five to ten pieces you wrote yourself
The most popular posts in your industry, so it copies what works
A prompt that tells the model to be a world-class copywriter
questions.explanation: The model needs your real writing to match. Have it describe your voice from your own pieces, correct what it gets wrong, and put two or three of them in the skill as examples.

questions.prompt: Which line is most likely to make a reader think AI wrote it?
options: "Order by 2pm and it reaches anywhere in Lekki today."
"My first order was my cousin's wedding. I was scared."
"It's not just a cake. It's a memory you'll treasure."
"₦25,000 for an 8 inch. People say it's not too sweet."
questions.explanation: "It's not just X. It's Y." is one of the patterns readers spot. The others are plain and specific: a time, a place, a price, a real detail.

questions.prompt: Why add "Use only the numbers I have given you" to a prompt for a client proposal?
options: It makes the model write the whole proposal faster and in fewer words
Proposals with fewer numbers are easier for clients to agree to
The model will then add a discount that helps you win the work
Models sometimes invent prices, discounts or terms you never offered
questions.explanation: A model filling gaps can add a discount or guarantee you never agreed to. Give it your prices and terms, tell it to use only those, and check every number before you send.

questions.prompt: In the landing page prompt, what is the [CHECK] instruction for?
options: It marks any claim the model had to guess, so you can fix or cut it
It tells the model to check your spelling and grammar as it writes
It adds a checkbox to the page so visitors can pick what they want
It makes the model check that the page works well on a phone screen
questions.explanation: Asking the model to mark guesses with [CHECK] catches invented claims before they go live. Replace each one with a true detail, or cut it.
